data.sourcePassage:
Britain was the first country to industrialise for several connected reasons. It had large deposits of coal and iron, which were vital fuels and materials for factories, machines and railways. Its island geography encouraged trade by sea, and its navy helped protect merchant ships and expand commerce worldwide.

Inventors and entrepreneurs combined to turn ideas into practical production. The spinning jenny, the water frame and improvements to the steam engine all helped make textile production faster and cheaper. Entrepreneurs like Richard Arkwright saw how to organise workers, machines and raw materials inside purpose-built factories.

Capital — money available for investment — also mattered. Profits from trade, farming and banking gave wealthy individuals the funds to build canals, factories and railways. Population growth provided both a workforce and a growing market of consumers. Agricultural improvements helped feed more people, and some rural workers moved to towns where industrial wages beckoned.

Britain's empire added another dimension. Raw cotton from overseas plantations — worked, in the key early decades, by enslaved labour — supplied British mills. Overseas markets bought British manufactured goods. Sea trade, finance, insurance and shipping all connected industrialisation to the wider world.

No single cause explains the Industrial Revolution. It happened because resources, technology, money, people, transport and global trade worked together in Britain at the same time.

questions.question: Which two natural resources were especially important to Britain's industrialisation?
options: Coal and iron
Gold and silver
Timber and wool
Cotton and rubber
questions.modelAnswer: Coal and iron were the two most important natural resources. Coal fuelled steam engines and furnaces, while iron was used for machines, rails and bridges.

questions.question: What was the role of entrepreneurs like Richard Arkwright?
options: They organised workers, machines and raw materials inside factories
They invented steam engines and built railways
They collected taxes for the government
They wrote laws to protect factory workers
questions.modelAnswer: Entrepreneurs organised workers, machines and raw materials inside purpose-built factories, turning inventions into large-scale production.

questions.question: How did Britain's empire contribute to industrialisation?
options: It supplied raw cotton and provided overseas markets for British goods
It provided steam engines and factory machinery
It ended the domestic system and forced workers into factories
It built all the canals and railways in Britain
questions.modelAnswer: Britain's empire supplied raw cotton from overseas plantations for British mills, and provided overseas markets where British manufactured goods could be sold.

questions.question: Why do historians say that no single cause explains the Industrial Revolution?
options: Because resources, technology, money, people, transport and global trade all had to work together
Because there were no important inventions during this period
Because Britain's empire was the only factor that mattered
Because coal replaced all other causes once it was discovered
questions.modelAnswer: Historians argue that industrialisation resulted from multiple causes working together — coal and iron, inventions, capital, population growth, agricultural change, transport improvements and imperial trade. Any single factor alone would have been insufficient.

data.sourceTitle: Life and Work in Industrial Britain
data.targetTitle: Life and Work in Industrial Britain
data.sourcePassage:
The factory changed what work felt like. Before factories, many textile workers had made cloth at home or in small workshops, fitting the work around family life and seasons. In the factory, the clock, the overseer and the machine set the pace. Workers arrived at fixed times, often before dawn. Long shifts of twelve hours or more were common. Fines punished lateness or mistakes.

Children were employed in factories and mines for practical reasons: they were small, cheap to hire, and poor families needed their wages to survive. Some children worked as piecers in cotton mills, repairing broken threads while machines ran. Others worked underground in coal mines, pulling trucks or operating ventilation doors in total darkness. Parliamentary investigations from the 1830s and 1840s collected disturbing evidence about their conditions.

The 1833 Factory Act was a landmark, banning children under nine from textile factories and introducing inspectors. The 1842 Mines Act banned women and girls, and boys under ten, from underground work. These reforms did not end hardship immediately, but they showed that Parliament could be pressured to protect workers.

For adult workers, wages, danger and working conditions varied. Skilled mechanics and engineers might earn decent wages. Unskilled labourers often struggled. Women were paid less than men for the same work. Trade unions and friendly societies gave some workers a way to organise and support each other, though unions were viewed with suspicion by many employers and politicians.

The question of whether industrialisation improved workers' lives has no simple answer. Some gained steady wages and access to cheaper goods. Many faced long hours, dangerous machinery, strict discipline and unhealthy towns. The impact depended heavily on class, skill, gender, age and location.

questions.question: How did the factory system change when workers could arrive and leave?
options: Workers had to arrive at fixed times set by the clock and employer
Workers could arrive whenever they wished
Workers only came in when machines needed repairing
Workers decided their own schedules at home
questions.modelAnswer: In the factory system, workers arrived at fixed times, often before dawn, and worked long shifts controlled by the clock and the overseer.

questions.question: Why were children employed in factories and mines?
options: They were small, cheap to hire, and poor families needed their wages
They were stronger than adults for factory work
The law required children to work rather than go to school
Factory owners preferred children because they worked faster
questions.modelAnswer: Children were employed because they were small, could be paid less than adults, and poor families often depended on their wages to survive.

questions.question: What did the 1833 Factory Act achieve?
options: It banned children under nine from textile factories and introduced inspectors
It ended all child labour in Britain immediately
It gave all factory workers a ten-hour working day
It banned women from working in cotton mills
questions.modelAnswer: The 1833 Factory Act banned children under nine from textile factories and introduced inspectors to check conditions. It did not end child labour immediately, but was an important reform.

questions.question: Why does the passage say there is 'no simple answer' to whether industrialisation improved workers' lives?

Because factories were always good for workers regardless of conditions
Because all workers earned the same wages in every factory
Because the reform laws solved every problem immediately

data.sourceTitle: The Impact of Industrialisation on Society
data.targetTitle: The Impact of Industrialisation on Society
data.sourcePassage:
Industrialisation did not only change work — it transformed where people lived and how towns were organised. Cities like Manchester, Leeds, Birmingham and Liverpool expanded dramatically. Manchester grew from roughly 20,000 inhabitants in 1750 to over 300,000 by 1851. This urbanisation brought people together in ways that created both opportunity and serious problems.

Housing in industrial towns was often built quickly and cheaply. Back-to-back houses with little ventilation, shared outdoor privies and polluted wells were common in working-class districts. Rubbish accumulated in streets. Factory smoke darkened the sky. Cholera and typhus spread through contaminated water. High infant mortality was a grim feature of early industrial towns.

Yet towns were also places of energy, community and change. Workers formed friendly societies and co-operatives to support each other. Chapels, public houses, markets and later libraries and parks gave urban life texture and meaning. Newspapers and pamphlets spread ideas about politics, religion and reform. Working-class communities developed their own cultures, identities and campaigns.

Railways transformed not just industry but society. From the 1830s, they connected distant towns, allowed people to travel who had never left their villages, moved newspapers and fresh food across the country, and began to standardise time itself. Railway building created enormous demand for coal, iron and labour.

By 1901, Britain was a highly urbanised, industrial society. Whether that represented progress depended entirely on who was asked. For factory owners and investors, industrialisation brought wealth and power. For many working-class families, it brought mixed blessings — steady wages sometimes, dangerous work often, and towns that were exciting and unhealthy in equal measure.

Around 100,000
Fewer than 50,000

questions.question: What were back-to-back houses?

Luxury homes built for factory owners near their mills
Houses built facing away from the street to reduce noise
Temporary wooden shelters for migrant workers

questions.question: How did workers in industrial towns create community despite difficult conditions?
options: They formed friendly societies, co-operatives, and attended chapels, markets and later libraries
They moved back to the countryside to escape the problems
They refused to work in factories and organised strikes every week
They relied entirely on the government to provide community spaces
